utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, as we understand the position, there is a dispute about the next witness, Mrs. Mahmutovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It relates to the late disclosure of her statement. I'll just make sure that I've got the facts right. The statement was taken on the 4th of March of this year from the witness and disclosed in English on the 5th of March, but the B/C/S translation was not disclosed until the 19th of May, some two days after the deadline.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, that is so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the objection is a late disclosure of these matters. Mr. Lopez-Terres, it's obviously better if the trial is conducted on the basis that the disclosure deadlines are adhered to. It makes life very difficult if they aren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, I quite understand your comment, Mr. President, but I can add the following as regards the situation with our witness, Mrs. Mahmutovic: The Prosecutor's office does not dispute that the Serbo-Croatian version of her statement was not disclosed to the Defence of Mr. Kordic and Mr. Cerkez until the 19th of May, that is, two days after the date as set by your decision of the 1st of April, and as you have quite correctly stated, the statement of the 4th of March, and then done in English on the 5th of March, was disclosed to the Defence. However, the Defence of the accused was informed of the intention of the Prosecutor to call Mrs. Mahmutovic by a letter of the 11th of June, 1992 (sic), and that letter was confirmed on the 18th of June, 1999. After this double confirmation, the Defence did not object. We did not receive any objection or any comment from them. In consequence, the Prosecutor's office believed they were authorised to undertake all the necessary preliminary steps so as to organise the testimony of Mrs. Mahmutovic. Likewise, may I add that the person who here wished to escort her here at the Tribunal during her appearance at the Tribunal, because Mrs. Mahmutovic was reluctant to appear by herself, this was done. The Victims and Witnesses Unit was accordingly advised, and it was only on the 29th of June that the Defence counsel of the accused Dario Kordic, and only Dario Kordic, let us know that they were opposing the testimony of Mrs. Mahmutovic. Now, I needed to explain all of this, but I should like to add also that the Prosecutor's office quite clearly believes that the objections of Mr. Kordic's counsel, and I'm repeating once again, by Mr. Kordic's counsel alone, is not, in our view, something that can be supported. Why do we think that this objection, this opposition, should be discarded? It is because Mr. Kordic's counsel, they all speak English, which is not always so in other cases that are before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, I'm going to interrupt you, and we'll just call on the Defence to hear what they've got to say about it. It's right, Mr. Stein, isn't it, that you have had notice since the 11th of June that this witness was liable to be called?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That is correct, Sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Stein, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That is correct. We were tied up with another issue that the Court put on us called the dossier issue, and I'm afraid that June 11th notice slipped through the cracks. However, on June 30th, when Mr. Scott made note that this witness was coming and there was a late translation, he asked us, by letter dated the same date, to give us his (sic) position no later that the close of business on Thursday, July 1, and we did that. So we gave him our position one would advance in an effort to diminish any travel inconvenience to the witness. Our position now, in the future and then, is that the Court's orders are clear, they need to be complied with. Prosecution knows they need to be complied with. If I take my colleagues' words, it seems that unless we speak up, the Prosecution deems that to be some sort of a waiver of our position. We're not going to waive that position. It was a Court-order-imposed deadline after much debate, after much discussion, and with the rights of the accused, and particularly the rights of the accused, to see the evidence in his own language in mind. Those are the rules of the case and the Rules of this Court and this Tribunal. Hence, we stand on our objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I apologise, Your Honours, but I also oppose the testimony of this witness on different grounds. We received the summary this morning. We were given the summary of this witness's testimony this morning, and it was a surprise from the summary that a considerable portion, I don't know how much, but I should say about one third of the summary is a completely new statement. These are from item 1 to item 20, apart from the two or three -- I mean the first ones which concern the witness, as such. I mean we see here some facts which were never mentioned in her earlier statement and the only statement of March 1999. In other words, we see here some new findings, and they are of major consequence for the accused Cerkez. We had absolutely no possibility of preparing ourselves for this. This is quite new, and we think that it is a completely new statement. What this is all about, we do not know whether another statement was given to the investigators or the Prosecutor directly and it has not been disclosed to us, or is it that the Prosecutor intends to use this summary to present the statements of this witness which they obtained from her during the past two or three days? This is something that we do not know, but this has nothing to do with the original statement of the witness of the 4th of May. The witness, in that statement, speaks about the events of the 16th of April, '93, and in only two or three sentences describes the events around that particular date, and here she is referring to some relevant events and facts which were happening at that time. This is, in substance, a completely new statement, and we are really opposing to this testimony because we simply had no opportunity of checking certain things, verifying them or supporting them, and we are simply unable to grapple with this kind of material. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We shall allow this witness to give her evidence now. But Mr. Lopez-Terres, we want to make it quite plain that in so doing, we are not in any way encouraging the Prosecution to be late in future with these statements and this disclosure, or to rely on, as it were, new witnesses. But in this particular case, we can see no real prejudice to the Defence arising from this witness being called, because notice was given as long ago as the 11th of June that the witness was to be called, and by then the statements had been fully disclosed. But we shall expect these matters to be attended to within the deadline, and because we are giving leave on this occasion, it doesn't mean that we will do so on every occasion. As for the matter which is raised by Mr. Kovacic, what we shall do is this, that cross-examination -- the witness can give evidence in chief. It will then be apparent if there is any new matter. If counsel requires time before cross-examination, Mr. Kovacic, then he can apply to postpone some part of the cross-examination until tomorrow afternoon, and he will have this evening and tomorrow morning to prepare. But I hope that won't be necessary. We'll call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we do, may I just change the record: We actually, according to our records, received the statement on May 21, a two-day difference. It's of no import to Your Honour's decision, but I want it to be clear. This will be a theme that will be coming up with other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, with regard to the disclosure of the translation, it was transmitted on the same day that we received it from the translation office. We received it on the 19th and we disclosed it on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Madam, you are Mrs. Nusreta Mahmutovic, born on 10th October, 1957; is that so?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And you are employed as a clerical worker in Zenica, you work for the Ministry of the Interior there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And you are with the department which is responsible for the issue of passports; is that so?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mrs. Mahmutovic, until April 1993, you lived in Vitez, in the quarter called Kolonija, on the street Podgradina, with your husband and your two daughters, aged 13 and 15 at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You were married to Mr. Saban Mahmutovic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Saban Mahmutovic was, for a period of time, deputy chief of police in Vitez at the time when there was a joint police force in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Saban Mahmutovic was a member of the SDA, was he?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Saban Mahmutovic never had any responsible positions in his party, did he?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, he did not really have any specific responsibility, any specific position, but he was a member of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Saban Mahmutovic, before he was appointed deputy chief of police in Vitez, was an inspector with the municipal administration of Vitez and was appointed chief of the uniformed police in Vitez following the elections of 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mrs. Mahmutovic, at the time that we are talking about, your husband, I suppose you knew which were the principal things that he had to do in his capacity of the chief of police in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, more or less, yes. I knew conversations among friends and what one could hear from -- one could learn in a normal conversation between a husband and his wife, between two spouses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Yes. You did not have to learn the detail; I mean, you were kept abreast of the events. And then in June 1992, the HVO hoisted the Croatian flag in front of the police station and then prevented various members of the police, and your husband, to enter their offices; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes, he told me that. I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did he also tell you, during those conversations that you had, that in October 1992 there was a meeting entered to try to reactivate the joint police station in Vitez, but that the police officers who were of Muslim origin were then asked to fill a form, to fill an application in which they were requesting to enrol in the HVO; is that so?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout that time, since about June 1992, my husband and other policemen of Bosniak ethnicity kept insisting on joint meetings so as to finally arrive at a joint police force. In October, when they believed that it would eventually happen, and that the police would become one again, at a meeting, there were first read -- rather, the then-chief, Samir, first read out them the wish, practically, in which they could become -- or rather go on working for the police administration in Vitez and said that if they wished to do so, they would have to fill the applications for the police of so-called Herceg-Bosna and thus give up their jobs with the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But they refused that. They were taken by surprise, and they thought they could somehow start with joint work. But after this instance and after -- and on the insistence on the chessboard flag, or rather the request that they apply for joining Herceg-Bosna, they refused and left the meeting. That is all that I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Your husband was deputy chief of the police in Vitez at the time, and the chief of the police in Vitez, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Muslim. Bosniak. A Muslim. You mean my husband, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: No, no, I'm talking about the chief of the police.

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, the chief of the police, himself, he was a Catholic. He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So the head of the police was a Croat, and your husband, as his deputy, was a Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So following the refusal to sign the application -- the form for the police of Herceg-Bosna, or the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, Muslim police officers then set up a separate commissariat in Stari Vitez, a separate station in Stari Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: It is, yes. They set up a police station in Stari Vitez. First they notified the centre of security service in Zenica, and the former police station in Vitez was at that time under the -- if I may put it so -- auspices of the centre for security services in Zenica. They explained what they were being asked to do, and they were issued additional instructions that Bosniak policemen could set up a separate police station in Stari Vitez, and my husband was the chief of that police station. He was appointed as its chief by the centre for security services in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And following that decision, there were two police headquarters in Vitez; is that so?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, as of that date, there were two police stations, and at that time, already, certain misunderstandings began to happen. If something happened in a place where the Muslims were a majority, then Muslim policemen would go out; or the other way around, if something happened in a place where Croats were a majority, then Croat policemen would begin to go out. And already at that time strife began, disputes began, because two police evidently could not work in one and the same place in one and the same direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mrs. Mahmutovic, during those conversations that you had with your husband at that time, you also heard there were some other attempts to reactivate the joint police force in Vitez, and he mentioned in particular a meeting which was held to this end on the 27th of July, '93, and I ask you to go through the report. I'm referring to the document which was already tendered before this meeting. It is Z340 (sic). Just a moment; you'll be shown the document.

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) It is document Z410.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you please read the document, Mrs. Mahmutovic. This is a document that has the name of your husband in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) This document has already been tendered to the Trial Chamber when witness Edib ^ Zlotrg testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, we have this document. It's already been produced, as you said. I don't think we need to spend any time on it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mrs. Mahmutovic, after you've glanced over the document, could you please tell us what happened and whether -- after this document was issued, was the police founded in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: A joint police station was never established from the day that the original police station broke up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Your husband, did he tell you at the time what the reasons were why this project was never implemented?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: The reasons were not acceptance of the police of Herceg-Bosna and the police markings with the chequered flag. This is something that the Bosniak police officers could not accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will continue. We're going to work on the next area. Is it true that in January, 1993, when you were at home, there was a strong detonation close to your house, after which there was no damage done to the building and nobody was injured? Could you please confirm whether this incident did actually take place?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, there were explosions. Mostly the facilities of Bosniak Muslims were blown up. Half an hour before this strong detonation was heard, the bank in Vitez was -- I can say it in my own words -- blown up. Very soon after that, maybe half an hour later, there was a strong detonation. I was in the house with my daughters, and I also had a refugee and her son. She was from Kljuc. We were very frightened. We didn't know that this was happening so close by. My husband wasn't there. I called the police station in Stari Vitez. I informed him what happened. Police officers came quickly, and this is all that I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: These explosions, these many explosions that you mentioned, could you please tell us, what was the purpose of these explosions and whose property was being blown up?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: These were Bosniak facilities, and the objective was to frighten the Bosniak population.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You said that the explosion which occurred near your house happened on the same night that the bank in Vitez was destroyed. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: A little bit before that, in February '93, somebody called you without identifying themselves at your house, and they threatened you, this anonymous caller threatened you. Could you please tell us what were the circumstances in which this call took place and what this anonymous caller said?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: The refugee woman who was staying with me from Kljuc, her husband was a member of the B and H army and he was on the front, on duty near Sarajevo. His unit was situated in Travnik, so on return from Sarajevo, from his duties, with a couple of his friends, a couple of his colleagues, members of the army, he stopped by our house. He just came to see his wife and his son. He was just passing by. He wanted to see them. They didn't enter the house. They were in the courtyard. Very quickly after that -- they only stayed for a short while, and they left towards Travnik, where their unit was located. Shortly after that, there was a telephone call. Ms. Besa answered. The person who was calling probably thought that I had answered the phone, because he addressed her with the words, "What are you doing, lady? What is that army at your house? You really should understand that your house is being watched. We know who is coming in and who is going out of your house. Don't try to do anything. There will be problems if something happens." Ms. Besa replied to that that this was the regular army, this was the army, and that was her husband who had just come simply to visit her.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Mahmutovic, I would like to you look at another document which was tendered earlier to the Trial Chamber. This is Document 3322. Would you please look at pages 4 and 5 of this document, which is in Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I would like to just say, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, that in the English version, these are pages 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So please would you look at page 4? On page 4, it states that, "On the 21st of January, at about 20 past 9.00, there was an explosive device which exploded close to the house of Saban Mahmutovic. His house is in Podgradina." Could you please confirm for us if this is the correct date and if it matches the events which you have already described for us?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember the exact date, but what I said happened in connection to the explosion did happen. It's all true. I don't remember precisely the date, but the police probably has the date in their report, and I believe that the date is correct. The event really did take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I would now, for the same reason, ask you to look at page 5 of the document, the next page, and the date "February 22nd, 1993". Do you see that section at the bottom of the page, where the date is "February 22nd, 1993"?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: On page 5, I see "February 21st".

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Page 5, at the bottom of that page, I will read the English version, which is on page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I would object. If I have the right document in hand, it's a witness statement of Mr. Zlotrg which was admitted for the purpose of impeachment only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a summary of the events in Vitez, which was introduced by one witness. It wasn't for the purpose of impeachment. I think it was introduced, as I recollect it, by the Prosecution. But I can't find where we're supposed to be in it. Which page are we supposed to be looking at, Mr. Lopez-Terres?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) In the English translation, it's page 8, and it's page 6 -- it's a bad copy -- in Bosnian, and it says "22nd of February, 1993". In English, it states, "On February 22nd, 1993, at about 6.00 p.m., we received a call from Saban Mahmutovic, indicating that he had received an anonymous call --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down. The interpreters do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) ... so a patrol was sent to the site. I would just like to ask Mrs. Mahmutovic whether the date of February 22nd matches the date that we had talked about.

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was looking at the English version, so I really couldn't find my way there. I found the bottom of the page. I don't understand what it states, but I did find the date, the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, let us not waste any more time on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: When we were talking about the period that we're discussing now, so January or February 1993, one evening the accused Mario Cerkez and Mr. Darko Kraljevic together came to your house. Could you please tell us something about that event?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can say, first of all, that I have never given such a statement before. I have said this in order to differentiate, because the person that I spoke to insisted he wanted to differentiate between the terms "army" and "police". In some documents, it was mentioned that my husband was a member of the army. According --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Mahmutovic, I'm going to interrupt you, if you don't mind, for a moment. Could you, just for the moment, tell us what happened when these two men came to your house? Don't worry about any statements or anything. Just tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: When Kraljevic and Cerkez arrived, it was -- I can't remember exactly, but it was quite late, maybe 10.00, 11.00 in the evening. It was night. They rang the doorbell. My husband came out. You could hear some shouting, some talk outside. On his return, when my husband came back, he told me that Kraljevic and Cerkez had arrived, and he conveyed to me that they were probably a little intoxicated and that the discussion was pretty noisy, but what they wanted was for my husband to get ready and to go in a car with them and to remove the checkpoints set up by the army. My husband didn't want to do this. He tried in every possible way to avoid going. He simply talked to them, and he told them that those checkpoints were not set up by the police, that they should go to the commander, Sefkija Djidic, to which they replied that they had already been to see him and that he had said that he could not remove those checkpoints, that Saban Mahmutovic was the only person who could do that. This conversation went on for about half an hour, perhaps. It was quite noisy. In the meantime, I had come out. I was surprised by the loudness of their discussion, by their loud talk. I came out and I addressed Cerkez. I told him, laughing, "What are you saying? Are you going to do something? Are you perhaps going to kill my husband?" I had something like that said sarcastically, but I only wanted to come out and see what was going on. And then Cerkez replied, "Well, I am not like that, Mrs. Mahmutovic, and nothing will happen to your husband." So I returned to the house. The conversation went on for a little while longer. I don't know in what manner, but ultimately my husband didn't go. He avoided going with them. I don't know what happened the next day regarding those checkpoints, but that night I know that the two of them had come and that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mrs. Mahmutovic, did you know the accused Mario Cerkez before he visited your house?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Personally, I didn't know him all that well. Mario Cerkez was a friend of my husband. I think that they worked together in the municipal office at one time, so everything that I can -- all that I can tell you regarding Cerkez, mostly I couldn't -- from conversations with my husband, my husband didn't really have anything bad to say about Cerkez. I simply had the impression that they were friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. On April 15th, 1993, your husband was invited to a party which was organised in Old Vitez, in the fire station hall, due to the anniversary of the B and H army, where he met the HVO representatives; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. They held a meeting there. The anniversary celebration was held there. They also reached an accord. I remember my husband came back towards evening. He was quite satisfied. He said, "Everything has been agreed. We will finally start working together, we will begin." So he was mostly quite happy with the outcome of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So your husband was quite optimistic, according to what you say; he had faith?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was convinced that this will start working and that everything will be all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: What happened the next day, on the 16th of April, in view of the events that we are familiar with?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: On April 16th, in the morning, we were woken up by explosions, detonations. My husband was in the house. I was in the house, too, and our children. I was working in Princip already, so I would leave for work earlier. My husband wasn't even up yet. I was already up. I had started to get ready for work. He said, "Just get ready. Everything will be okay. These are just some small clashes, some small misunderstandings." He simply didn't consider that a conflict would -- a broader conflict would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Returning to the evening of the April 15th, did your brother, Nusret Kalco, come to visit you that evening?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my brother came. He had listened to Dario Kordic's conference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's an objection. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: This is double hearsay, and as you can see from the proffer before you, it's double hearsay of vague statements attributable to my client without a time, place, or substance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, would you like to ask some questions, before dealing with the statements themselves, as to how it is that this witness heard about them?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mrs. Mahmutovic, your brother visited you on April 15th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Your husband talked to him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: My husband, yes, he talked to him. My brother had come with the intention of telling us to leave Vitez, that something terrible was about to happen. He had heard on the television Kordic's press conference, and he was suggesting that we leave Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: With respect, I would like to ask the examination to proceed normally as a direct, as opposed to leading, and we lead up to this point, which is where Your Honour's ruling --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me deal with it. Did you yourself, Mrs. Mahmutovic, hear anything that had been said on the television?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't watch television, but I heard what my brother had told my husband. My husband replied to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: "You're too frightened."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Take it slowly.

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You heard your brother had told your husband, who told you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was there. He came to our house, my brother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were present when he was telling your husband about what had been said?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, besides the hearsay nature of this, the statements on television have to be put in time/place context, one statement two or three weeks before, the week before, the day before, and they are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll admit this evidence. Whatever weight is to be given to it is, of course, something we will have to decide. Perhaps you could get some more detail about it, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So, Mrs. Mahmutovic, you stated that you didn't personally hear those statements on the television, so could you tell us, according to your understanding, when did Mr. Kordic make those statements on television? Was that that same day?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: My brother came in the evening on the 15th. He came to tell my husband that based on what he had heard at the press conference of Dario Kordic, that some conflicts could come about, a bad situation could happen, so he was suggesting that we leave that part of Vitez, to which my husband replied that everything was okay. "We had agreed already. Don't be so frightened. What's the matter with you." And he simply talked to him, and we didn't go out that evening. We stayed at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what your brother's duties were at that time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: My brother was the director in Princip, in Vitezit. I think it was called Princip.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. We had started to talk about the events that took place on April 16th, in the morning, so chronologically I will just remind you of that. You said that after you were woken up by explosions, you had decided, at the suggestion of your husband, to go with your children to a neighbour's house, Dr. Patkovic, and then to the house of a Croatian friend, Mr. Ramljak, where there was a shelter. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Your husband remained in your house, and then he came to join you after a while at Mr. Ramljak's house; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: After that, he left you and he hid again, because that morning he had decided to hide?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: At the end of the morning, late in the morning, you had decided to go back to the house to get some clothes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: When you went back to your house, you saw a group of ten HVO soldiers. Some of them were in camouflage uniforms, some were wearing black uniforms, and they had taken up positions around your house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You heard, from the house, soldiers who were discussing and asking themselves whether they should shoot before they entered the house or not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You opened the door of your house. The soldiers came in, and one of the soldiers asked the others, "Who is his wife"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: These soldiers pointed their weapons at you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Your friend, the refugee that we already mentioned, was with you, and one of the soldiers indicated at you, and he said, "Yes, that's her. She's the older one"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Those soldiers asked you where your husband was?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Then they put you in a room, and while one of the soldiers was guarding you in that room, the rest were searching the house; is that true?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During the search of your house, did you hear the soldiers talking and mentioning your husband?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: The soldiers climbed to the second floor of our house. They were searching. They were cursing our balija mothers. They were saying, "Look at this crook. He really situated himself well. Look at all the things that he has in his house," and they were using bad abuses, they were hurling abuses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Then you left your house. Could you tell us, when you left, what did the soldiers say, what were the words that some of them used?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: One of the soldiers, and he was the leader of that group, but let it be clear it was an organised group sent to our house with a purpose, he said, "What shall we do with them?" The one who was standing guard over us said, "Well, let them go. Forget about them. They are women and children." The one who I think was the HVO soldier and the leader of the group, he said -- well, just described it. He said, "You'll lose your heads." We came out in front of the house. We didn't know where to go, so we just stood there until one of those soldiers said, "What are you waiting for? You'll get the next bullet." Then we went down the street and got to Nafiz Patkovic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Before you left your home, could you see what the soldiers were doing? Were they using their weapons before that? Did they take over your house?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I've never seen so much hatred. I never believed there could be so much hatred, that one could destroy something with so much hatred. They were firing. There were bursts of fire. It was like fireworks that went out at the front of the house, at the back of the house. It was terrible. It was awful. It was frightening to watch them, what they were destroying, how they were destroyed, and how much hatred they put into the destruction of that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: What eventually happened to that house, Mrs. Mahmutovic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, finally as we were still there, the curtain in the nursery began to burn. My house has burnt down completely, and in the shelter in which we were, we could see our house burning. My late husband also saw that, and he knew that his house had burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So your house was completely destroyed that day?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, completely burnt down, down to the foundations, and it was a big house, a three-storey house, a new one. We had moved into it barely three years before that. It had been razed to the ground. That is what human hatred and malice can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: After those events which you just described to us, you told us that you returned to that Croat, Mr. Ramljak, who offered you shelter, and then in his house you found soldiers who had been to your house also came to that Croat's house. Now, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can say -- that is what I can say about that man, because he really is a proper -- Vlado Ramljak took us in as his own. He took us to his shelter. As we were in the shelter, that same group came to Vlado's house, saw me and my children, and the leader -- I mean the man that I believe was his leader, a tall, fair-haired young man, perhaps 22 or 23, turned to Vlado and said, "Vlado, you look after that Saban's wife and children while his men are killing Croats. Up there they're killing Croats." That is what he said then. Mr. Vlado said that he simply could not summon either the strength or heart to throw us out because we were children and women, and that this one was a soldier, he knew what he had to do, but that he --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: -- Vlado Ramljak, that is --

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: -- could do nothing but just try to help women and children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, I think the next part need not be dealt with in a great deal of detail. There are no doubt distressing matters, and we don't need to stress them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) There was just something which I wanted the witness to specify, although I know that all these events are very painful, but it has do with the death of Mr. Saban Mahmutovic, because Mr. Saban Mahmutovic died in Vitez during those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mrs. Mahmutovic, you were not present when your husband died, but you heard about it from witnesses, about the circumstances of his death; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: It is, yes. We were in Mr. Vlado's shelter when the house was set on fire. We saw the house burning. We knew that my husband was in the house, but all that we could think about at that moment was that he had burned down together with the house. We did not know what was going on. My children were next to me, and crying, and I was hugging them, but we did not want to show them that my husband was in that house. And then subsequently, from witnesses, from my brother, from my former friend Ivanka Biletic were heard, about the circumstances when the house was burnt down. And if you want me, I can tell you. I can tell you that my house was put fire to. My husband was in its loft. He jumped from the balcony of the loft to the balcony of the middle floor, and from the middle floor, when the fire, when the flames had reached it, threatening him, he jumped from that middle balcony, which was rather high up. He jumped down, but the house was surrounded by HVO soldiers. He jumped down and started to run towards the wood behind the house, but they caught up with them. And my brother was watching from Vlado Ramljak's loft, how they beat them, how they battered him. They were kicking him mostly in the area of his stomach. He simply could not walk. They were dragging him, they were dragging him from that house towards -- he assumed towards the shelter, towards people, or the camp, I don't really know what to call it, but towards the place where they were detaining all the Bosniaks they had taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clear explanation. I do understand that it is very difficult for you. Mrs. Mahmutovic, you could not personally see your husband's body because you left Vitez before his funeral, but have you heard about the state in which his body was?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, there were people from Vitez, from the authorities, people who had tapes who saw it, who knew it, who saw the body. I avoided -- I shunned talking to people about that, even though on a couple of occasions I could see that tape, I refused it; I simply couldn't brace myself to do it. And from my husband's brother's son, who was a policeman in Stari Vitez, he was buried in Stari Vitez, he saw his body, and he wanted to tell me, but I gathered that -- that was his assumption, that the whole part of his face and mouth was missing. They guessed that perhaps they had put a grenade into his mouth and it was blown off. At any rate, I mean, parts of his face was missing, and I simply didn't want anyone to show it to me or tell me about it. I simply refused to hear of any more details. If you really want to know about it, you can look for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much, madam. I want now to show you a document which is a death certificate, which is Z2233. Mrs. Mahmutovic, you have this document before you; could you please confirm to us that this is the death certificate of your husband, Saban Mahmutovic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is the death certificate of my late husband, but the date of his death is not correct. The place, yes, it is correct, and all the other particulars are correct, but my husband was killed on the second morning, because they could not find him; he was very well sheltered in the loft. And this document, I had this document, I needed it -- or rather all the families needed those documents in order to regulate various matters, the status of combatants killed. It was the municipality which was issuing this, and the majority of Bosniaks, of Muslims, of eminent Bosniaks in the authorities perished on the 16th, so this was also done on the 16th. But I have the 17th. I have this correction, the 17th, and indeed he was killed on the 17th. That would be correct. I think the hour is correct here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: But this document is your husband's death certificate; everything is correct except the date of the -- except the date of his demise, the 17th rather than the 16th?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mrs. Mahmutovic, did you know of the death of other persons whom you knew in Vitez or other fellow policemen of your husband on that date, the 16th of April, 1993? And if you did know of other such cases, do you know their names?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Mr. Vlado's shelter, the news arrived all the time: So-and-so has been killed, so-and-so has been killed. Amongst the first was the news of the death of Midhat Varupa, the representative of the Bosniak authorities, and he was killed because groups were sent specifically to kill eminent Muslims. In addition to Midhat Varupa, I know that Salem Topcic was killed. That was a very close colleague and friend of my husband's. He was an inspector with the Ministry of the Interior. He was stabbed to death before his wife and his children. Nedim Zlotrg and his wife, Mira, they were also killed in their house, also before their children, and the mother of--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I know you object to this. The witness is merely repeating stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's nothing in the statement about it; I quite agree. We are able to give such evidence what weight it's worth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, would you perhaps control the witness to some extent, so that we stick to what is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I should like to show four documents to the witness and ask her -- these are death certificates, and I shall ask her to tell us whether they contain the names of those persons. It is 2232 -- 2210, two and 22 ten three?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do have before me the death certificate of Mr. Nedim Zlotrg. That is correct. His wife, Mira Zlotrg; I can also confirm that she was killed that same day. Salem Topcic, that same day. Midhat Varupa. They were all people killed on the first day, and they were amongst the first to be killed, and these are indeed those individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There will be no objection to the death certificates.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: They speak for themselves. As to whether this is the appropriate person to authenticate them, I make that comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is a comment and no more. We will admit it. Yes, let's move on, shall we? What I would like to do, if at all possible, is to finish the evidence in chief before the adjournment which we'll take at 4.00, and then, if possible, deal with the cross-examination this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, that will be possible, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mrs. Mahmutovic, after the facts that you just described to us, the death of your husband, you and your two daughters could not find any shelter in Vitez because nobody was ready to shelter you, to help you, and so you were forced to wander for about -- several days after that fact, and around the 20th of April, 1993, that is, some four days after the event, you were captured with your daughters by HVO soldiers near the UNPROFOR base at Divjak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And the HVO soldiers then decided to exchange you for the bodies of some HVO soldiers from that area?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Before, however, this exchange, and the UNPROFOR acted as the intermediary, you said that your daughters and you were subjected to -- were exposed to comments, to sarcastic remarks, jokes, and even threats by those HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, which were the threats, exactly, that you received?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, and I don't know how many of them there were, because HVO soldiers were coming in all the time, but Dragan Budimir and Braco Budimir -- "Braco" was his nickname; I do not know his true first name -- but they could be singled out. We sat on a bench outside in a line. Mr. Besa's son, me, my two daughters, and soldiers would come from behind our backs, and one would sit in front of us and aim his rifle and say, "Well, Besa, you lived with them, you'll die with them." Or then he would approach one of my daughters from the back and would say, "I'm about to strangle one Saban's daughter; I'm about to strangle another daughter." They will hang me on the pillar, on the lamppost. They used expletives, balija this or that, shalom aleicheim (phoen), but using it in a pejorative way. At any rate, a very difficult situation, very unpleasant. Children cried, and it was very difficult, very tense all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And at a given moment while you were facing those soldiers, you saw the accused, Mario Cerkez arrive; could you tell us about the circumstances under which he arrived and his relationship with those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: To be quite honest, on the basis of everything and on the basis of conversations, although such conversations were not all that frequent -- I mean in relation to Cerkez -- it was my feeling that my husband was a close friend with him. And when I heard that Cerkez was coming, because those soldiers said, "Here comes Cerkez," and I saw Cerkez coming from the UNPROFOR base down the asphalt, and a couple of soldiers from Vitez. When I saw him I was, truth to tell, very happy to see him. I don't know really why. I somehow felt that this would result somehow that he would help me -- Mario Cerkez, I mean. I probably was obsessed with that idea and anticipation. But Mario Cerkez was coming in our direction, and there were those soldiers. He never cast a look at us. He never cast a single glance at me or my children. He approached the soldiers, and those HVO soldiers were mad, were furious. They were cursing our balija mothers, toward the five of us and my dead husband, because there were some dead Croats. They were cursing. I went towards Mario one or two metres; I mean, that is how far he was from us. And I heard him say, "As far as I'm concerned, you can slay them all." Because if they were threatening us in front of them and saying they would do this or that, I mean, everything they said before him, he answered to that, "Yes, you can slay them, but they are all on the list. The UNPROFOR is here, BBC is here, so the Armija would gain a major advantage because of that." This is what Mr. Cerkez said within the hearing of both me, my children, and all those present. He never turned and addressed us, even though I fervently hoped that he would. Perhaps I was too naive. I thought -- I hoped that Mario Cerkez could be the man to help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And the next night, you and your two daughters were exchanged; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And you left that night?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: That night, that very night, we were exchanged, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And you left to Zenica. Could you --

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you tell us, at the time as you left Vitez, could you take some clothes or some of your personal affairs with you when you left?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Those HVO soldiers who had broken into my house did not allow me to take anything. I wanted to take just a jacket; they would not allow me. So I left the house in slippers, with nothing else. I mean, we just left with things that we had on, both me and my children. We crossed a hill in order to reach Zenica. We lost everything. I really don't know what else to tell you. If you have any other questions, I really -- I mean, it was all horrible. It was all really terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you help us with this, Mrs. Mahmutovic: On the 15th of April, when your brother came to the house and was talking about what he had heard Dario Kordic say on the television, can you remember what it was that he said? Can you remember what it was that Dario Kordic had said? Or if you can't -- I don't want the words, but what was it, in general terms?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: In general terms, he said -- my brother heard, and he came to warn my husband. He said that as far as he could understand his speech was that a conflict was unavoidable, and he urged us to go to -- to withdraw to Stari Vitez or to Preocica, which was a Muslim village. My husband refused it. He said everything was all right, they had reached an agreement, and there would be no problem whatsoever. And so we stayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What happened to your brother?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: My brother went through all that we went through, at the advice of a Croat friend of his who gave him shelter that night and the next night. And he said, "Well, the next morning, when the HVO soldiers come, surrender, because that will be the only way to save your life." If only he would surrender and allowed to be taken to that place, wherever, where Muslim Bosniaks were taken and detained. So he did that, and Patkovic, Dr. Patkovic did the same thing. They surrendered and were put up in the cinema hall in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now. As I said, I hope it's going to be possible to complete cross-examination this afternoon, since the witness is here, and it would be better if we could deal with her now. Very well. We'll adjourn, we'll break for a quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, with your permission, the two Defence teams have conferred, and in view of the fact that you offered us the possibility of postponing this part of the examination referring to new elements of evidence we had not heard about before, our suggestion would be as follows so as not to waste time, and that is for the Defence of Mr. Kordic to start with the cross-examination. I will continue when they finish, and, with your leave, after some introduction, I wouldn't follow the same order but would go on to the summary of the part of the evidence which contains the statement of the witness made on the 4th of March. By then, we will have come to the end of the day, and then tomorrow I could go on to the part which is new, so that I would be cross-examining in continuation but I wouldn't follow the chronological order. Of course, with your permission, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need to follow the chronological order. You can follow whatever order you think appropriate. I had hoped we might be able to finish the witness today, but let's see how we get on. Yes, Mr. Naumovski. Are you going to go first, Mr. Kovacic? Who is going first?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Perhaps it would be better for Mr. Naumovski to start, because he will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Your Honours. Mrs. Mahmutovic, allow me to introduce myself. I am Mitko Naumovski, attorney from Zagreb, Defence counsel for Mr. Kordic. I have several questions for you, and would you be kind enough to answer them for me. Before that, just a note of caution. As we speak languages we both understand, will you please not answer me straightaway but wait for a few seconds for my question to be interpreted into French and English, and then give your answer. I shall also do the same and try to make a pause between the questions and the answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mrs. Mahmutovic, you gave a statement to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal on the 3rd and 4th of March this year?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: As noted here, you made that statement to the best of your knowledge and recollection; is that true? Will you please speak into the microphone and a little louder so that everyone can hear you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You also signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The statement was signed in the English language. I assume it was interpreted back to you first.

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mrs. Mahmutovic, will you tell us, apart from this statement, did you ever make any statements to anyone else?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: When I left Vitez and reached Zenica, people in the MUP, as my husband worked in MUP, I gave statements to them. But for The Hague, I gave that statement, as you have said, on the date that you have indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So am I right in saying you made a statement about what had happened in Vitez to the Centre of Security Services in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was only natural. As soon as I left with my children, I was taken in by the Ministry of the Interior. I explained to them everything that had happened. That was during that same year in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Apart from that statement, did you make any other statement to any other body of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I do not remember anything of any importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. In this statement that we just mentioned, the only one that you gave to The Hague Tribunal's investigators, you never once mentioned Mr. Kordic; would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Today in this courtroom, you mentioned for the first time what your brother was saying in your house on the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That is the first time you have said that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I said that also when I came here to the gentleman I spoke to, because the discussion went in that direction. In order to prove how certain my husband was that there would be no conflict, I said that. That is why I said that my brother came and said that a conflict was in the offing on the basis of Kordic's statement. That is what I said. If you consider this to be something new, as far as I'm concerned, it was always present, even then in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I know you spoke to the Prosecutor, because we received this morning a summary with questions indicating what you were going to talk about, and that is why it was very interesting to learn from whom you heard about the things that were discussed in your house on the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Do I need to repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let me explain to you why I'm asking you that. In this statement, in this summary that we have, it was explicitly stated that this was said to your husband; not to you, to your husband. That is why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, that is a play of words that you're highlighting. I was there in my house when my brother came in. Now, whether I said this or that to the Prosecutor, I'm telling you now I heard my brother come and say to my husband to get ready. "I heard Kordic's words at his press conference, and in his words, war is inevitable."

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, and that is what you told His Honour the President, your brother conveyed to you his conclusion about what he had heard on television?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is how he understood the press conference, and he appealed to my husband to leave, to take shelter, because the majority were Croats and we were in danger, and especially people with any positions. My husband did not accept that. He didn't believe that would happen. My husband did not hear that press conference, but he said, "Everything will be all right. We've come to an agreement. Don't panic."

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you're going to tell me again that I'm formalistic, but from the summary that I have reminded you of, mention is made of several statements on television, not just one single press conference.

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, sir, I personally had occasion to watch television and to hear Kordic's words even before then. Those words indicated even before that a conflict could break out. His words only sowed discord among people. You do not have to stick to that particular reference that I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Will you please answer my question? I'm talking about the 15th of April, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So let us try and clarify this. Did your brother tell you when he saw that programme and on what TV channel?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you. It was probably then, because he was upset when he came to our house, and his purpose in coming was to warn my husband to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Naumovski, is there really, on the Defence side, any challenge of the existence of this television programme and of this televised speech by the accused Mr. Dario Kordic that has already been referred to? This is not the first time it has been mentioned. You're not challenging this, so there's no need to spend so much time on something that appears to be a point of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I understand Your Honour, what you're telling me, but I am the Defence counsel who was given a statement and found in it what he did find, and now I am faced with a witness who is saying something slightly different. So I'm trying to distinguish between facts and conclusions. I understand Mrs. Mahmutovic's conclusion to be that judging by her brother's appearance and attitude, that he had heard that programme that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That was your conclusion, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can't tell now. I didn't think that that would be necessary, that that would be asked of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: No, no, that's fine. Everyone is entitled to his own conclusions. Tell me, please, did you discuss this any time later with your brother?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No. About those details, no, we never discussed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, please, I don't wish to insist, but just a few questions relating to your husband's job. I didn't quite hear you say when this new police station was formed in Stari Vitez. Could you tell us roughly?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't give you the exact date. It was in October, I know that, because it was an important session that took place when they expected unification. Whether it was January or when, I really can't say, but I'm sure that there are people who can give you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you must know how many men were involved.

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: All the policemen. I don't know the exact number. All the Bosniak policemen who used to work in the police administration in Vitez joined, each and every one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did your husband wear a uniform when he went to work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, with the insignia of police, the police station. At first, they wore the standard police uniforms, and then afterwards, they wore camouflage uniforms with the patch saying "Police".

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So it was a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Speaking about your husband's work and what your husband told you about his work, mention was made of an event when a checkpoint needed to be removed. Do you know how many checkpoints were held by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina or, rather, the civilian police in the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't tell you those details. These were events that were discussed among friends and colleagues, and I learned about them from those contacts. This particular case of a checkpoint was something I wanted to tell about, because Cerkez and Kraljevic came to try and remove it, to show that my husband was a policeman and not a member of the army. And that is why I made this additional statement, to make it clear to the gentlemen that my husband was a policeman, and that was the purpose of that statement, because it was set up by the army. How many there were, how many were set up by the police, how many by the army, I really can't tell you. I don't know, nor was I interested. I know about the event that happened in my own house, which I told the investigator about, to show that my husband was first a policeman and then a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, please, where was this checkpoint that you discussed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I really don't know. There were probably several checkpoints that needed to be removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I understood that you spoke about one, and that's why I'm asking you which one.

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: All I know is that there was reference to those checkpoints that particular night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: If I understood you well, you lived in a part of Vitez inhabited by Croats, who were the majority, and your husband went to work in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So I assume there were other policemen working with him who lived in this part.

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Jazek (phoen), who was here as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you talk to that witness after he came here?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you will agree that these other policemen also wore uniforms when they went to work?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the weapons that the police were issued. I know that my husband had a pistol. He also had a rifle. I really can't go into the weapons that the police had at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mrs. Mahmutovic, you never personally met Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, I have no more questions. Thank you, Mrs. Mahmutovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Mahmutovic, allow me to introduce myself. My name is Bozidar Kovacic. I'm an attorney from Rijeka. My colleague is Mr. Mikulicic, and we appear on behalf of Mr. Cerkez. As Mr. Naumovski has already told you, we understand one another but we have to bear in mind that everything we are saying is being interpreted, so wait a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I think our conversation functioned well, or do you think that I need to slow down even further?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) A couple of seconds would be welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, here, in answer to some introductory questions, you said that you worked in the MUP, in the Ministry of the Interior. That is the police, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you're working in the police?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is that the federal police or is it the Zupanija police?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: It is the Ministry of the Interior. For me, that is the federal police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any Croats working in the same service?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The ethnic composition is fully reflected as regards Croats and Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that is already functioning in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, madam, when the Serb aggression started in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what citizenship did you have?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The republican citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When Bosnia-Herzegovina, in April 1992, became a sovereign state, what citizenship did you have then?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: The same, the same citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So throughout that time, you were a citizen of the same country, which changed its identity, but still --

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Are you a practising believer?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Of the Islamic faith?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Mario Cerkez before the war?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How well did you know him?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Not that well, but I knew him. I would meet him in the street. My impression was that he was a good friend of my husband's, and through their friendship, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have any other common friends?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed, we did. You mean Croats?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Either Muslims or Croats.

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From all those contacts, could you tell us, until the beginning of the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats, did he show any signs of nationalist intolerance towards the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So there were no signs of that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I could even list you his friends who were the same age as he, that is true, but there were many Croats who were friends of his with whom he was as close as a brother. Karlo Karin (phoen), Cerkez knows him very well, not to mention others. With Cerkez too, I thought he was on good terms, and I could give you other names. They don't occur to me now because seven years have gone by since.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, madam, did you know any other members of the Cerkez family?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: No, not really. I knew Cerkez through my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know what citizenship he had at the time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it was Bosnian, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, if I understood you correctly, the place where you lived, or the street, Podgradina, and you yourself said that, is part of Vitez known as Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that would be on the fringe of Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, more -- yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would it be true to say that among the buildings within that area known as Kolonija, there are two cafes next to another, one called 072 and the other Benz; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the course of '92 and '93, until this conflict on the 16th of April, 1993, did you see soldiers gathering there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, there were some soldiers, but I really wasn't interested in those soldiers in those days. I never even noticed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You didn't notice that these cafes were gathering places for certain circles?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Then, no, but during the conflict, I personally saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean after the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may ask you, what is it that you saw in connection with those cafes?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: You mean during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I lived there, and my daughter's friend went to school with my daughter. Her mother took me in. I stayed with them, and I saw from their apartment people gathering, all kinds of people, people in black uniform, in camouflage uniform. I had the feeling that this was a kind of meeting place. I remember very well the conflict in Ahmici. That night, Marijan Dinac came. He was some sort of an organiser. "The soldiers will come back. We have succeeded." I personally saw this. I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The Vojica (phoen) apartment is nearby where you were at the time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, right next to those cafes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The soldiers gathering there, did they wear any particular insignia?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC
utterances.text: I've already told you, they were soldiers wearing different insignias, and what I saw in particular was the colour of the uniforms. I couldn't really see the insignia worn by each individual soldier. Most of them were HVO soldiers. Some were wearing black blouses, and what insignia they wore, I really couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
